cases.case_name: Cechman v. Travis
cases.holding: The court held that OCGA 19-7-5 creates no private civil cause of action and that, even if it did, the reporting duty is triggered only for a physician who actually has reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused and who then knowingly and willfully fails to report, so summary judgment for the physician was correct.
cases.quote: The statute requires that notice be given only by those physicians "having reasonable cause to believe that a child has been abused"

relevance.INP-01: This is Georgia's leading construction of the mandatory-reporting statute that defines when a designated reporter's duty actually attaches.
relevance.INP-02: It explains that the reporting statute is a penal provision that does not itself generate civil liability for anyone who reports or fails to report.
relevance.INP-06: It confirms that the statutory reporting scheme, including hotline intake, is enforced criminally rather than through private damages suits.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from an emergency-room encounter and fixes the trigger for a treating physician's reporting duty.
relevance.INP-08: The same 'reasonable cause to believe' trigger governs the school personnel listed in OCGA 19-7-5.

cases.case_name: Ray v. Department of Human Resources
cases.holding: The court reversed, holding that a juvenile court may order disclosure of otherwise confidential DHR child-abuse records when it finds disclosure necessary to resolve an issue before it, and that parental rights may not be terminated on a bare 'welfare of the child' test without a showing of parental unfitness.
cases.quote: it is not proper to consider the question of termination of parental rights based solely upon a "welfare of the child" test, without some required showing of parental unfitness

relevance.INP-01: It shows that the confidential report file generated by a mandated report can be reached by court order when fairness requires it.
relevance.INP-04: It is the Georgia authority for a court compelling production of agency investigative records in a proceeding it is hearing.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated agency finding does not substitute for judicial proof of unfitness, and the file behind it is discoverable on court order.
relevance.DEC-05: It sets the substantive floor the Department must meet once it petitions: unfitness, not merely a better home elsewhere.
relevance.OUT-05: It is a Georgia example of an agency case collapsing because the unfitness showing was absent.
relevance.FAIL-06: It identifies the statutory mechanism by which confidentiality of child-abuse records yields to a court's need for the information.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the Georgia precedent for judicially compelled access to otherwise sealed child-protection records.

cases.case_name: Georgia Department of Human Services, Division of Family and Children Services v. Steiner
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the superior court and upheld the central child abuse registry as applied, holding that listing as a substantiated abuser did not, on this record, satisfy the stigma-plus test and so triggered no federal procedural due process protection, and that 'some evidence' supported the ALJ's substantiation.
cases.quote: Steiner failed to demonstrate a constitutionally protected liberty or property interest sufficient to trigger the due process protections that he claims were violated by operation of the registry

relevance.DEC-03: This is the controlling Georgia decision on what process a substantiated abuse finding and registry listing require.
relevance.DEC-01: It describes the screening-to-substantiation pathway and the administrative hearing that follows a founded finding.
relevance.INP-02: It sets out how reports are intake-screened and how the resulting classification is contested.
relevance.INP-06: It describes the confidential intake and substantiation system built on reports received by DFCS.
relevance.INP-08: The substantiated finding at issue arose from a school-connected allegation and shows the consequences for the named adult.
relevance.INP-10: It maps the escalation from report to investigation to substantiation and administrative review.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading modern example of a Georgia court reviewing, and here restoring, an agency's substantiation decision.
relevance.FAIL-05: It rejects the claim that registry listing is punitive and requires criminal-style protections.
relevance.FAIL-06: It confirms that registry records and the associated administrative hearing are sealed from the general public.
relevance.PMC-03: It shows that review of Georgia substantiation decisions runs through an ALJ and the courts, not a citizen panel.
relevance.PMC-05: It confirms the statutory sealing of registry records and hearings, a direct constraint on transparency requests.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the baseline authority for any systemic analysis of Georgia's substantiation and registry data.

cases.case_name: Georgia Department of Human Services v. Spruill
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the Court of Appeals and held that the Georgia Tort Claims Act's discretionary function exception preserved sovereign immunity for a DFCS caseworker's choices in investigating a report of child neglect, barring the tort suit brought after the children were severely injured.
cases.quote: But when such agents act as representatives of the sovereign, they exercise a different sort of discretion, one that may be informed in significant part by considerations of public policy.

relevance.DEC-02: It is the controlling Georgia authority on the discretion a caseworker holds once a report is accepted for investigation.
relevance.DEC-01: It holds that decisions about how far to take an investigation, including closing it out, are discretionary and immune.
relevance.INP-01: It traces what happens after a pediatrician's mandated report reaches DFCS and who bears the loss if the response fails.
relevance.INP-02: It addresses the state's liability exposure for how it handles a received report of neglect.
relevance.INP-06: It confirms that response-time and face-to-face-contact policies are guidance, not immunity-stripping mandates.
relevance.INP-07: The report at issue came from a treating pediatrician, and the case defines the state's duty in responding to it.
relevance.INP-09: It shows that DFCS policy manuals do not create judicially enforceable investigative duties.
relevance.INP-10: It is the leading Georgia case on the discretion exercised when a screened report is escalated to investigation.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the controlling Georgia immunity rule when children are gravely harmed after a DFCS investigation.
relevance.OUT-06: It governs tort recovery in Georgia when a child suffers catastrophic injury following an agency investigation.
relevance.PMC-01: It shows that Georgia's performance failures in investigation are not remediable through state tort litigation.
relevance.PMC-04: It is the Georgia decision a fatality or near-fatality review must reckon with on accountability for investigative choices.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of C. C.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia vacated and remanded, holding that the juvenile court applied the wrong standard in finding the parents' religious objection to immunization insincere, and declining on constitutional-avoidance grounds to decide whether OCGA 15-11-30 transfers the right to make religiously freighted medical decisions to DFCS.
cases.quote: Thus, when the Chandlers consented to the adjudication of dependency, they were consenting to the transfer of those parental rights for the duration of DFCS's custody.

relevance.ACT-06: This is the Georgia Supreme Court's most recent statement on DFCS authority to obtain medical care for a child in its custody over parental objection.
relevance.ACT-03: It explains exactly which parental rights pass to DFCS as legal custodian when a child enters foster care.
relevance.ACT-02: It shows that a consented dependency adjudication transfers decision-making authority for the life of the case.
relevance.INP-07: It governs medical decision-making, including immunization, for children already in agency custody.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of M. F., a Child
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed dismissal of a father's petition, holding that under OCGA 15-11-244(c) a change in a parent's circumstances sufficient to make a previously unfit parent fit can be a material change in the child's circumstances warranting modification, vacatur or revocation of a permanent guardianship.
cases.quote: We hold only that a change in parental circumstances sufficient to render a previously unfit parent fit may constitute a material change in the circumstances of the child.

relevance.OUT-03: It is the controlling Georgia rule for reopening a permanent guardianship entered as the permanency outcome.
relevance.ACT-04: It governs the durability of a kinship or third-party guardianship once the parent's situation improves.
relevance.INP-05: It is the vehicle by which a rehabilitated parent may ask the juvenile court to restore custody.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of B. R. F., a Child
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the Court of Appeals could not itself excuse an untimely discretionary application in a termination case; an indigent parent whose appeal was frustrated by ineffective assistance must first ask the juvenile court, which decides whether counsel was constitutionally required under Lassiter and whether an out-of-time application is warranted.
cases.quote: Thus, litigants in this state cannot obtain relief from an order terminating parental rights by filing a direct appeal.

relevance.FAIL-01: It fixes the only route by which a Georgia parent can undo a termination order tainted by counsel's default.
relevance.OUT-02: It governs appellate access after a Georgia termination judgment, including the ineffective-assistance remedy.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of I. L. M.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that although a juvenile judge may continue an adjudication hearing on his own initiative, the continuance and the nunc pro tunc order entered here had to rest on matters actually before the court and comply with the governing statutes.
cases.quote: No such statement is present here, and so we conclude that a judge may consider a continuance on his or her own initiative.

relevance.DEC-05: It controls the timing and record requirements once a dependency petition is filed and the adjudication hearing is continued.
relevance.INP-04: It addresses the juvenile court's own initiative in managing a dependency proceeding it is hearing.

cases.case_name: In re Baby Girl Eason
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that an unwed biological father has a constitutionally protected opportunity interest in developing a relationship with his child, and that if he has not abandoned it he must be judged by a parental fitness standard rather than a best-interests standard before his child is adopted away.
cases.quote: unwed fathers gain from their biological connection with a child an opportunity interest to develop a relationship with their children which is constitutionally protected

relevance.OUT-02: It is the foundational Georgia authority on a biological father's standing to block an adoption and the standard applied to him.
relevance.INP-05: It establishes the interest a previously uninvolved parent may assert when he comes forward to claim his child.

cases.case_name: Drummond v. Fulton County Department of Family & Children Services
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed dismissal of long-term foster parents' suit to block removal of their foster child, holding that foster parents acquire no legal right to the child, no right to adopt over the agency's withheld consent, and no Fourteenth Amendment property or liberty interest from the foster relationship.
cases.quote: foster parents have no right to adopt a foster child and thus no right to contest the agency's withholding of consent

relevance.ACT-03: It defines the legal position of Georgia foster parents relative to the agency that placed the child with them.
relevance.ACT-04: It forecloses a claim of entitlement based on length of caregiving alone, including by non-relative caregivers.
relevance.OUT-03: It holds that a psychological-parent relationship does not by itself create permanency rights in Georgia.
relevance.OUT-04: It confirms that a foster placement, however long, confers no protected interest in the child's continued placement.

cases.case_name: In re M. A. F.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed, holding that a caregiver who had received parental power by a valid relinquishment contract and stood in loco parentis was entitled to the notice, hearing and juvenile-code safeguards that the juvenile court denied her before the child was removed and custody given to the agency.
cases.quote: The juvenile court failed to acknowledge the appellant's rights, and undoubtedly failed to provide her with the safeguards and procedures of the juvenile code

relevance.DEC-04: It condemns removal of a child from a lawful custodian without notice or a hearing.
relevance.INP-12: It is the Georgia authority that emergency custody transfers still require the juvenile code's procedural safeguards.
relevance.INP-05: It recognizes the standing of a private caregiver who took the child in at the parents' request.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the Georgia Supreme Court's treatment of a removal accomplished without the required notice and hearing.
relevance.ACT-04: It protects a non-parent caregiver holding parental power by relinquishment contract against summary displacement.
relevance.OUT-03: It recognizes in loco parentis custody as a durable permanency status the juvenile court must respect.
relevance.ACT-05: It shows that orders altering custody must issue only after the statutory notice and hearing.

cases.case_name: Southeastern Legal Foundation, Inc. v. Ledbetter
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that clinical records made confidential by OCGA 37-3-1(2) fall outside the Open Records Act's disclosure command, so the newspapers could not obtain a state hospital patient's mental health records under that Act.
cases.quote: the disclosure provisions of OCGA § 50-18-70 (b) do not apply to clinical records as defined by OCGA § 37-3-1 (2)

relevance.PMC-05: It is the Georgia rule that a separate confidentiality statute removes records from the Open Records Act entirely.
relevance.PMC-02: It limits what a public-interest requester can extract from a state human-services agency by records request.
relevance.FAIL-06: It identifies the statutory mechanism agencies invoke to withhold human-services records from the public.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of R. G.
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed a nonreunification order, holding that clear and convincing evidence of the mother's unjustified failure to comply with a previously ordered reunification plan raised the statutory presumption against reunification services, which she had not rebutted.
cases.quote: Reunification services are not required when reasonable efforts to reunify a child with his family would be detrimental to the child.

relevance.ACT-02: It is the Georgia standard for court-ordered case plans and the consequence of non-compliance with them.
relevance.ACT-01: It shows that voluntary engagement in services is measured against the plan's concrete goals, not effort alone.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the controlling Georgia authority on when reunification ceases to be the permanency goal.
relevance.DEC-06: It marks the boundary at which service-based, non-adversarial handling gives way to a nonreunification finding.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of R. S. T., a Child
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals vacated a termination order and remanded, holding that the Department failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that continued dependency would cause the child serious harm, because it must show harm both from return to the parent and from remaining indefinitely in foster care.
cases.quote: The Department must show that both scenarios would likely cause serious harm in order for a termination of parental rights to be justified.

relevance.OUT-02: It states the fourth, most frequently missed element of Georgia's termination standard.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a recent example of a Georgia appellate court vacating a termination for unsupported findings.
relevance.OUT-05: It shows the evidentiary failure that ends a Department case short of termination.
relevance.ACT-02: It ties the serious-harm analysis to the parent's engagement with the ordered case plan.
relevance.OUT-01: It requires the court to weigh the harm of leaving a child in care rather than returning her home.
relevance.DEC-05: It defines what the Department must ultimately be able to prove when it opens and escalates a dependency case.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of T. C.
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's rights, holding that imprisonment alone does not authorize termination but that his failure to support the child while in prison, his lack of any relationship with the child, and his conduct after release were aggravating circumstances supporting the finding that dependency would continue.
cases.quote: the father's failure to support T. C. while in prison and his lack of relationship with the child may be considered aggravating circumstances

relevance.OUT-02: It is the Georgia rule for terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent and what counts as aggravation.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of K. M., a Child
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that a juvenile court deciding a parent's petition to end a third party's temporary guardianship must apply the clear and convincing evidence standard for physical or significant long-term emotional harm, not a probable-cause standard, and that the burden rests on the third party seeking to keep custody.
cases.quote: the burden of satisfying this stringent standard rests on the third party who is seeking to obtain or maintain custody of the child

relevance.OUT-03: It sets the standard and burden for dissolving a kinship guardianship and returning the child to a parent.
relevance.ACT-04: It governs the relative caregivers' burden when the parent seeks the child back.
relevance.ACT-01: It shows that a consensual, service-oriented guardianship does not shift the burden onto the parent later.
relevance.INP-05: It is the route by which a parent who earlier consented to a guardianship asks for the child's return.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of D. L. T.
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed placement of two siblings in the Department's permanent custody with their foster family rather than with paternal grandparents, holding that after termination there is no conclusive relative preference and the juvenile court has wide discretion to weigh the children's best interests, including their sibling bond.
cases.quote: Following the termination of parental rights, juvenile courts are not obligated to attempt to place a child with relatives, but need only consider the best interests of the child.

relevance.ACT-04: It is the Georgia rule that the relative-placement preference is a consideration, not a mandate.
relevance.OUT-03: It governs the choice between kinship permanency and adoption by a foster family after termination.
relevance.OUT-02: It addresses post-termination placement, including keeping siblings together with prospective adoptive parents.
relevance.ACT-03: It confirms the juvenile court's discretion to keep a child in a stable foster home over a relative's claim.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of A. C.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reached and rejected the father's constitutional challenge to OCGA 5-6-35(a)(12), holding that requiring a discretionary application to appeal a termination order violates neither due process nor equal protection, and affirmed the termination of his parental rights.
cases.quote: fundamentally no equal protection violation can exist unless legislation treats similarly-situated individuals differently

relevance.FAIL-01: It upholds the procedural gateway that every Georgia parent must pass to obtain review of an agency-driven termination.
relevance.FAIL-05: It rejects the equal-protection attack on treating terminated parents differently from parents who lose custody temporarily.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of C. R.
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the deprivation finding as to the mother but reversed the award of temporary custody to DFACS, holding that a temporary loss of custody requires clear and convincing evidence that the parent is unfit, and here only the mother's unfitness had been shown.
cases.quote: There must be clear and convincing evidence that the parents are unfit to support a grant of temporary custody to DFACS.

relevance.DEC-05: It states the proof the Department must carry to convert a dependency finding into agency custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It shows that removal to agency custody must be justified as to each parent, not the household generally.
relevance.ACT-03: It is the Georgia rule limiting placement into foster care to cases of proven parental unfitness.
relevance.ACT-05: It illustrates the less restrictive alternative of leaving the child with a fit parent under protective conditions.
relevance.INP-04: It reviews the shelter-care order and dependency petition together as the court-supervised entry point of the case.
relevance.INP-12: It reviews the order for shelter care alongside the deprivation petition and fixes the proof required.
relevance.OUT-01: It requires re-evaluation on current circumstances before custody continues away from a fit parent.
relevance.OUT-05: It is a Georgia example of an agency custody award being undone for failure of proof.
relevance.DEC-06: It shows that where only one parent is unfit the case need not proceed to agency custody at all.

cases.case_name: Doe v. Kearney
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit upheld warrantless emergency removal against facial and as-applied attack, holding that due process permits removal without prior judicial authorization where there is probable cause of imminent danger, and rejecting a rule that the caseworker must separately find there was no time to obtain a court order.
cases.quote: Having considered all relevant factors, courts may then decide whether an objectively imminent danger justified the state's removal of a child without prior judicial authorization.

relevance.DEC-04: This is the governing Eleventh Circuit standard for removing a child before any court order issues.
relevance.INP-12: It defines the constitutional limits on emergency protective custody in the circuit that includes Georgia.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the benchmark against which a Georgia removal is measured for Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment purposes.
relevance.INP-03: It governs officers and caseworkers acting together on an emergency report of danger to a child.
relevance.ACT-05: It frames when a protective response short of removal suffices and when exigency justifies immediate custody.

cases.case_name: Loftus v. Clark-Moore
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal on qualified immunity, holding that social workers who interviewed a minor without her father's consent and threatened removal during a child abuse investigation violated no clearly established Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment right.
cases.quote: Because neither social worker violated any clearly established federal civil rights in the investigation that Loftus had invited, we affirm the dismissal of Loftus's complaint against them.

relevance.DEC-02: It is the Eleventh Circuit's clearest statement on the constitutional limits of investigative interviews and consent.
relevance.INP-10: It addresses what investigators may do once a report is escalated to a full child abuse investigation.
relevance.INP-08: It governs interviewing a child without parental consent, the recurring school-based investigation problem.
relevance.INP-03: It defines the constitutional latitude of investigators cooperating on an abuse report.
relevance.FAIL-02: It shows that threats of removal, without a removal, do not themselves defeat qualified immunity.
relevance.INP-01: It shows the investigative response that follows a professional's report and the immunity investigators enjoy.

cases.case_name: Taylor v. Ledbetter
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc in a case against Georgia DHR and DFACS officials, the Eleventh Circuit held that a child involuntarily placed in foster care has a Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process liberty interest in safety, and may sue under section 1983 where officials acted with deliberate indifference.
cases.quote: The state's failure to meet that obligation, as evidenced by the child's injuries, in the absence of overriding societal interests, constituted a deprivation of liberty under the fourteenth amendment.

relevance.ACT-03: It is the foundational circuit authority defining the state's constitutional duty to children it places in foster care.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the controlling framework for liability when a child is gravely harmed in Georgia foster care.
relevance.OUT-06: It supplies the deliberate-indifference standard applied to serious injury or death in state custody.
relevance.OUT-04: It defines the state's continuing obligation for as long as the child remains in its placement.
relevance.ACT-06: It grounds the agency's affirmative duty to secure care and protection for a child in its custody.

cases.case_name: H.A.L. ex rel. Lewis v. Foltz
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of qualified immunity, holding that on the alleged facts the defendants knowingly exposed children in state-supervised care to a substantial risk of serious harm and were deliberately indifferent to that known risk, conduct Taylor had already clearly established as unconstitutional.
cases.quote: Defendants knowingly subjected the children to a substantial risk of serious harm and exhibited deliberate indifference to the known risk: conduct already clearly established as unconstitutional

relevance.FAIL-04: It is the modern circuit application of deliberate indifference where children were sexually abused in care.
relevance.OUT-06: It shows what pleading suffices to reach a jury after serious harm to children under agency supervision.
relevance.OUT-04: It confirms the state's duty persists throughout the time children remain in its care arrangements.
relevance.PMC-04: It is the litigation counterpart to a fatality or near-fatality review of a supervised placement.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that before a State may irrevocably sever the rights of parents in their natural child, due process requires proof of its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence, and struck down New York's fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: Thus, at a parental rights termination proceeding, a near-equal allocation of risk between the parents and the State is constitutionally intolerable.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal constitutional floor for the standard of proof in every Georgia termination case.
relevance.DEC-03: It marks the constitutional difference between an administrative preponderance finding and severing parental rights.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the standard against which a Georgia termination judgment is measured on review.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, and left the appointment decision to the trial court in the first instance, subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: It supplies the federal counsel standard that Georgia's juvenile courts apply in termination proceedings.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the source of the case-by-case inquiry Georgia courts must run before an ineffective-assistance remedy attaches.
relevance.DEC-05: It frames the parent's right to representation from the moment the State petitions to sever the relationship.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a state's failure to protect a child from violence by his father, even after repeated reports and agency monitoring, is not a deprivation of liberty under the Due Process Clause, because the Clause imposes no general affirmative duty to protect.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause.

relevance.DEC-01: It is the controlling federal rule when a screened-out or closed report is followed by harm to the child.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the threshold barrier to constitutional claims when a child dies while known to the agency but at home.
relevance.OUT-06: It distinguishes harm in state custody from harm in the home for constitutional liability purposes.
relevance.FAIL-03: It confirms that federal constitutional law does not itself enforce agency performance standards.
relevance.PMC-04: It is the case any fatality review must confront on the limits of legal accountability for non-removal.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that states make reasonable efforts to prevent removal and reunify families creates no right enforceable by private individuals under section 1983 or directly under the Act.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the controlling holding that federal child welfare compliance is enforced through funding, not private suit.
relevance.ACT-02: It establishes that the federal reasonable-efforts mandate is not privately enforceable against the agency.
relevance.ACT-01: It shows that federal prevention-service expectations do not create individual entitlements to services.
relevance.PMC-01: It explains why CFSR performance failures are addressed administratively rather than in private litigation.
relevance.PMC-02: It locates enforcement of federal child welfare funding conditions with the Secretary rather than private plaintiffs.
relevance.PMC-03: It confirms that federally required oversight structures do not themselves confer private rights.
relevance.PMC-06: It is the baseline for understanding what federal non-compliance findings can and cannot produce.
relevance.INP-09: It explains why oversight findings, not lawsuits, are the mechanism for federal child welfare compliance.
relevance.DEC-06: It confirms that the federal prevention-services framework does not compel any particular front-end response.

cases.case_name: Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody, that section 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where the termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family, and that section 1915(a) preferences do not bar an adoption where no preferred placement has come forward.
cases.quote: we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights

relevance.INP-11: It defines when ICWA's heightened termination and active-efforts requirements actually attach in a state proceeding.
relevance.OUT-02: It controls the termination and adoption analysis whenever the child is an Indian child under ICWA.
relevance.FAIL-05: It addresses the racial-classification concerns raised by applying ICWA based on minimal Indian ancestry.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that 'domicile' in ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, that children born off-reservation to parents domiciled on the reservation are themselves domiciled there, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction, voiding the state adoption decree.
cases.quote: We therefore think it beyond dispute that Congress intended a uniform federal law of domicile for the ICWA.

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling authority on exclusive tribal jurisdiction and on transfer under ICWA sections 1911(a) and (b).
relevance.INP-04: It shows that a state court must resolve ICWA jurisdiction before proceeding, whatever the parents' wishes.
relevance.OUT-02: It voids state termination and adoption decrees entered without ICWA jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court rejected all challenges to ICWA, holding that Congress had authority to enact it, that the anticommandeering challenges failed, and that the equal protection and nondelegation challenges could not be reached for lack of standing, leaving ICWA and its placement preferences fully operative in state courts.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: It confirms that Georgia juvenile courts remain fully bound by ICWA's requirements and placement preferences.
relevance.FAIL-05: It leaves unresolved, for lack of standing, the equal protection attack on ICWA's placement preferences.
relevance.ACT-04: It preserves ICWA's placement preferences, which override ordinary state kinship-placement practice for Indian children.

cases.case_name: M. L. B. v. S. L. J.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that a State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to pay record preparation fees, and must provide a record of sufficient completeness for appellate review.
cases.quote: we hold that Mississippi may not withhold from M. L. B. "a 'record of sufficient completeness' to permit proper [appellate] consideration of [her] claims."

relevance.FAIL-01: It guarantees indigent parents meaningful access to appellate review of a termination judgment.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal rule ensuring that poverty cannot foreclose review of a termination decree.
relevance.FAIL-05: It treats wealth-based exclusion from termination appeals as a due process and equal protection violation.

cases.case_name: Clark v. Wade
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed and remanded two grandparent-versus-parent custody cases, upholding the best-interest standard of OCGA 19-7-1(b.1) as constitutional only under a narrowing construction requiring the third party first to prove by clear and convincing evidence that parental custody would harm the child, and only then that third-party custody would best promote the child's welfare and happiness.
cases.quote: the third party must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the child will suffer physical or emotional harm if custody were awarded to the biological parent

relevance.ACT-04: It is the Supreme Court of Georgia's controlling construction of the harm standard a relative caregiver must satisfy to keep a child against the parent's claim, and the doctrinal parent of the K. M. and D. L. T. line.
relevance.OUT-03: It fixes the constitutional floor for any kinship or third-party permanency arrangement in Georgia: harm to the child, proved by clear and convincing evidence, not a bare comparison of homes.
relevance.INP-05: It governs the reverse path, where a parent who let relatives take the child comes forward to reclaim custody and the third party bears the burden of defeating the parental presumption.

cases.case_name: Boddie v. Daniels
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed and remanded, holding that Clark v. Wade's narrowing construction controls the 'best interest' standard in OCGA 29-2-8(b), so a juvenile court may not deny a parent's petition to terminate a third party's temporary guardianship without finding by clear and convincing evidence that termination would cause the child physical or significant long-term emotional harm.
cases.quote: Therefore, the juvenile court erred by denying the petition to terminate the temporary guardianship without finding by clear and convincing evidence that such termination would harm the child.

relevance.INP-05: It is the Supreme Court of Georgia authority protecting the parent who voluntarily consented to a guardianship during a crisis and later asks the court to give the child back.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the controlling Georgia rule for returning a child home from a third-party guardianship, placing the burden on the guardian rather than on the parent seeking reunification.

cases.case_name: State v. Jackson
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed a declaratory judgment striking down Georgia's former central child abuse registry, holding that a person classified as a confirmed abuser has more than a reputational interest at stake and that the statute's absolute bar on compelling testimony from a child under 14 denies due process in a large fraction of cases, so the entire Act, OCGA 49-5-180 et seq., had to fall.
cases.quote: The portion of OCGA § 49-5-183.1 that precludes an accused from compelling a child's testimony in the administrative proceedings is unconstitutional and central to the general scope of the Act

relevance.DEC-03: It is the Supreme Court of Georgia's first and most searching examination of what process a substantiation classification requires, and it must be read alongside Steiner, which reached the opposite result on a different record and a rebuilt statute.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the Georgia decision holding that the confidentiality and closed-hearing architecture of the abuse registry cannot be maintained on procedures that deny the accused the ability to test the evidence.
relevance.PMC-05: It shows that Georgia's registry confidentiality scheme has itself been held constitutionally defective once, which is the starting point for any transparency analysis of the current recodified registry.
relevance.INP-10: It sets out in detail the statutory path from completed investigation through the unfounded, unconfirmed and confirmed classifications and the administrative hearing that follows.

cases.case_name: Nix v. Department of Human Resources
cases.holding: Answering a question certified by the Court of Appeals, the Supreme Court of Georgia held that an indigent parent whose rights were terminated by a juvenile court on a state agency's petition is entitled to a transcript at public expense to appeal, because the Juvenile Code was designed to give such a parent effective representation at all stages of a termination proceeding.
cases.quote: The answer to the certified question is, yes — such a parent is entitled to a paupered copy of the transcript.

relevance.DEC-05: It is the source of the Georgia rule that the Juvenile Code guarantees an indigent parent effective representation from the moment the State petitions to sever the relationship, not merely appointed counsel on paper.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the Georgia forerunner of M. L. B., ensuring that an indigent parent is not priced out of appellate review of a termination order, and it is the authority B. R. F. relies on for the statutory-ineffectiveness theory it left open.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of M. D. H.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia resolved a conflict between two Court of Appeals panels, holding that when the State misses the 30-day petition-filing deadline of OCGA 15-11-521(b) without obtaining an extension the case must be dismissed without prejudice, because the 2014 Juvenile Code's silence about the consequence of a missed deadline does not authorize the extreme sanction of dismissal with prejudice.
cases.quote: when a Juvenile Code statute is silent in this way, Georgia appellate precedent holds that the consequence is dismissal without prejudice

relevance.DEC-05: It is the controlling rule on what happens when the State blows a statutory filing deadline after a complaint is lodged: the petition is dismissed, but the State may start over within the statute of limitation.
relevance.INP-12: It construes OCGA 15-11-521 alongside the detention timelines, and collects the line of cases (Sanchez, E. C.) holding that missed emergency-custody and petition deadlines produce dismissal without prejudice rather than release from further proceedings.
relevance.OUT-05: It defines what a Georgia dismissal for missed statutory deadlines actually accomplishes, which is a closure that does not bar refiling.

cases.case_name: Bendiburg v. Dempsey
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: In a Georgia case the Eleventh Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that whether DFACS employees' ex parte transfer of custody and consent to a Hickman catheter over the father's objection satisfied procedural due process turns on whether a genuine medical emergency existed, and that private physicians and nurses who reached an understanding with the caseworkers to obtain that order may be liable under section 1983 as joint actors.
cases.quote: Parental autonomy may be limited when parental decisions jeopardize the health or safety of a child, and the state can intercede on the child's behalf.

relevance.ACT-06: It is the leading Georgia-based federal authority on agency-authorized emergency medical treatment over a parent's objection, and on the limits of that authority when the emergency is manufactured or exaggerated.
relevance.DEC-04: It holds that an ex parte custody transfer obtained without notice is constitutionally tolerable only in extraordinary circumstances and only where a meaningful post-deprivation remedy is genuinely available.
relevance.INP-07: It arises directly from a medical encounter in which clinicians escalated a treatment disagreement into a DFACS referral, and it defines what clinicians may and may not do in that posture.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the section 1983 conspiracy framework by which private clinicians who feed false exigency to caseworkers become liable for an unlawful custody deprivation.
relevance.INP-12: It fixes the constitutional standard for protective custody obtained by ex parte order in Georgia juvenile court, including the adequacy of the post-deprivation probable-cause hearing.

cases.case_name: Floyd County Grand Jury v. Department of Family & Children Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed an order quashing grand jury subpoenas to seven DFACS employees, holding that county departments of family and children services are instrumentalities of the state Department of Human Resources rather than county offices, so a grand jury has no power under OCGA 15-12-71(b)(2) or any other statute to conduct a civil investigation of DFACS.
cases.quote: these departments are instrumentalities of the Department of Human Resources (DHR), a state agency, independent of the county, and no evidence has been presented to the contrary

relevance.INP-09: It is the controlling Georgia authority on who may and may not audit a county DFACS office, and it forecloses the grand jury as a civil oversight mechanism over child welfare operations.
relevance.FAIL-06: It shows that a disclosure or transparency demand aimed at DFACS must be addressed to the state, not the county, and cannot be compelled by county-level investigative process.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the closest real Georgia child-welfare authority on outside access to DFACS records and personnel, and it identifies the structural obstacle a records requester faces.
relevance.PMC-02: It establishes that DFACS is a state instrumentality funded through state and federal channels, which locates financial audit authority at the state and federal level rather than with the county.
relevance.INP-04: It marks the outer boundary of compulsory process directed at DFACS by a body other than the court hearing a child's case.

cases.case_name: Perdue v. Kenny A. ex rel. Winn
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed the Eleventh Circuit in the Georgia foster-care class action, holding that a lodestar fee under 42 U.S.C. 1988 may be enhanced for superior attorney performance only in rare and exceptional circumstances supported by specific evidence, and that the district court's 75 percent enhancement was not properly justified.
cases.quote: In the present case, the District Court did not provide proper justification for the large enhancement that it awarded.

relevance.PMC-01: It is the United States Supreme Court's decision in the very litigation that produced Georgia's foster-care consent decree and its independent accountability agents, and it governs what plaintiffs' counsel can recover for driving that kind of systemic reform.
relevance.PMC-02: It sets the federal standard for scrutinizing the public cost of structural child-welfare litigation against a state agency, and is mandatory subsequent history for anyone citing the Eleventh Circuit's Kenny A. fee decision.

cases.case_name: Mandt v. Lovell
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed, holding that a family violence permanent protective order under OCGA 19-13-4 is a continuing judgment that a superior court retains power to modify or terminate after the term of court has expired, but only where the restrained party proves by a preponderance of the evidence a material change in circumstances making resumption of family violence unlikely.
cases.quote: For that reason, a PPO should not be impervious to future modification if the underlying balance has substantially changed.

relevance.ACT-05: It is the Supreme Court of Georgia's governing decision on the family violence protective order, the principal Georgia mechanism for separating an abuser from a household without removing the child, and it fixes both the order's duration and the standard for dissolving it.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of J. C. W.
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals vacated and remanded a juvenile court order awarding long-term custody of twins to their maternal aunt and uncle until their eighteenth birthday, holding that OCGA 15-11-58(i)(1) contains no statutory preference in favor of relative placement and that the juvenile court's contrary legal conclusion may have tainted its exercise of discretion.
cases.quote: Because OCGA § 15-11-58 (i) (1) contains no preference in favor of relative placement, the juvenile court erred by finding otherwise.

relevance.OUT-04: It is the closest Georgia appellate authority on the eighteenth-birthday terminus of a child-welfare custody disposition, holding that a long-term custody order runs to age 18 and that the children themselves are real parties in interest who may appeal it.
relevance.ACT-04: It holds that the pre-2014 Juvenile Code's list of dispositional options creates alternatives, not a priority ranking, so a relative placement must be justified on the child's best interests rather than on kinship alone.
relevance.OUT-03: It governs the choice among long-term relative custody, continued foster care and a referral for termination and adoption as competing permanency outcomes for the same child.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read; quotes were machine-verified as exact substrings of the retrieved majority opinion text after whitespace and quotation-mark normalization.

The key_cases already present in the GA node files are keyword-matched noise - almost all are Supreme Court of Georgia attorney-discipline matters (In the Matter of ...) with synthetic citations. None were retained. The only real lead among them, S25G0338 In the Interest of M. R. S., returned no retrievable opinion text on CourtListener in this session and was therefore excluded.

Georgia's Central Child Abuse Registry statutes cited in the node files (OCGA 49-5-180 to 49-5-187) were repealed and reserved by Ga. L. 2020, p. 181 (HB 993), effective July 1, 2020; the registry now sits in OCGA 49-5-40 et seq. Ga. DHS v. Steiner, 303 Ga. 890 (2018), decided under the earlier Article 8 scheme, remains the controlling due-process analysis and should be read together with the 2020 recodification.

No Georgia appellate decision applying the Indian Child Welfare Act was located in this session in either the Supreme Court of Georgia or the Court of Appeals of Georgia. Georgia has no state ICWA statute. INP-11 is therefore mapped to the three controlling United States Supreme Court decisions (Holyfield, Adoptive Couple, Brackeen), which bind Georgia juvenile courts directly.

No published Georgia decision was found on extended foster care or juvenile-court jurisdiction past age 18 (OUT-04). That node is mapped to the Eleventh Circuit foster-care-safety line (Taylor, Ray v. Foltz, H.A.L.) plus Drummond and Kenny A., which define the state's duties and the class of youth in care. A lawyer should treat OUT-04 as governed by OCGA 15-11-340 to 15-11-341 and the Georgia Independent Living Program rules rather than by case law.

No Georgia case law was found on CFSR monitoring, Citizen Review Panels under CAPTA 5106a(c), or the federal child fatality review commission (PMC-01, PMC-03, PMC-04). Those nodes are mapped to the federal standard - Suter v. Artist M. (federal child welfare requirements are not privately enforceable), DeShaney, and Kenny A. (structural consent-decree oversight of Georgia's foster system) - plus Spruill for state-law accountability. This is a genuine gap in on-point authority, not an omission.

No Georgia appellate decision was located on family-violence protective orders used as an alternative to removal (ACT-05), on anonymous-tip reliability at intake (INP-06), or on children who go missing from Georgia foster care. ACT-05 and INP-06 are mapped to the closest available authority (Kearney and C. R. for protective alternatives; Cechman, Spruill and Steiner for the intake and substantiation chain).

Kenny A. ex rel. Winn v. Perdue is included for its factual record of the Georgia foster care consent decree and its thirty-one outcome measures and independent accountability agents; its actual holding is an attorney-fee ruling, and the quote reflects that. It should not be cited for any substantive child-welfare rule.
Taylor v. Ledbetter is cited in its 1987 en banc form, 818 F.2d 791, which reversed the 1986 panel decision at 791 F.2d 881. Do not cite the panel opinion.

Cechman v. Travis is the Court of Appeals' construction of OCGA 19-7-5 as it stood in 1991; the statute has since been amended (including by Ga. L. 2012, p. 239) and the current version should be checked for the reporter list, the 24-hour reporting deadline and the express immunity provision in OCGA 19-7-5(f)-(g), on which no Supreme Court of Georgia decision was located in this session.

In the Interest of R. S. T. and In the Interest of K. M. were reported in S.E.2d only in the CourtListener cluster data available in this session; their official Ga. App. volume and page were not present in the retrieved cluster records, so the citation is given in the S.E.2d form with a court designator.

The date_decided values are the date_filed values recorded in the CourtListener cluster records. For Lassiter that record is 1981-08-28 (the amended-opinion date); the opinion is conventionally cited as decided June 1, 1981.

All Georgia dependency cases decided before January 1, 2014 use the former Juvenile Code's term 'deprived' rather than 'dependent'; In the Interest of M. F., 298 Ga. 138, 142 n.2, treats the distinction as immaterial for these purposes.
No unpublished or memorandum decisions were used.

Missing (for a later pass): Perdue v. Kenny A. ex rel. Winn, 559 U.S. 542 (2010) — mandatory subsequent history. The Supreme Court reversed the very fee enhancement the brief reports Kenny A., 532 F.3d 1209, as affirming. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2358, decided 2010-04-21). Citing the Eleventh Circuit opinion as good law without this flag is a citator failure; if the consent decree and its thirty-one outcome measures are the point, cite the district court decree proceedings instead.

Missing (for a later pass): Clark v. Wade, 273 Ga. 587, 544 S.E.2d 99 (2001) — the Supreme Court of Georgia's leading construction of OCGA 19-7-1(b.1), governing parent-versus-third-party custody and the harm standard a non-parent must satisfy. It is the doctrinal parent of the K. M. and Boddie line the brief does cite, and its absence leaves ACT-04, OUT-03 and the kinship nodes resting on intermediate appellate authority.

Missing (for a later pass): Boddie v. Daniels, 288 Ga. 143, 702 S.E.2d 172 (2010) — the Supreme Court of Georgia decision on the best-interest standard when a parent seeks to terminate a third party's temporary guardianship under OCGA 29-2-8. K. M., which the brief relies on for OUT-03 and ACT-04, is largely an application of Boddie and quotes it repeatedly; the brief cites the application without the controlling authority.

Missing (for a later pass): State v. Jackson, 269 Ga. 308, 496 S.E.2d 912 (1998) — the Supreme Court of Georgia's earlier child abuse registry decision, holding that stigmatization of reputation alone does not implicate a liberty interest. Steiner expressly builds on it ('We followed this directive... in State v. Jackson'), so DEC-03 and FAIL-06 are incomplete without it, particularly given the 2020 repeal and recodification of the registry articles.

Missing (for a later pass): Nix v. Department of Human Resources, 236 Ga. 794, 225 S.E.2d 306 (1976) — the Supreme Court of Georgia on an indigent parent's entitlement to effective representation at all stages of a termination proceeding. B. R. F. relies on it for the statutory-ineffectiveness theory it leaves open, so FAIL-01 and DEC-05 are missing the source of the Georgia rule the brief's own lead case discusses.

Missing (for a later pass): In the Interest of M. D. H., 300 Ga. 46, 793 S.E.2d 49 (2016) — the Supreme Court of Georgia's construction of the 2014 Juvenile Code's dependency timing and dismissal consequences. I. L. M. cites it for exactly the OCGA 15-11-181(a) proposition the brief's I. L. M. entry omits; DEC-05 and INP-12 need it.

Missing (for a later pass): Bendiburg v. Dempsey, 909 F.2d 463 (11th Cir. 1990) — a Georgia case holding that a DFCS caseworker who conspired with a physician to obtain a court order authorizing a medical procedure without parental consent could face section 1983 liability. It is the obvious authority for ACT-06 (emergency medical care) and DEC-04, and is cited in Maddox, which the brief already uses. ACT-06 is currently left with a single case because this is absent.

Missing (for a later pass): Floyd County Grand Jury v. Department of Family & Children Services, 218 Ga. App. 832, 463 S.E.2d 519 (1995) — Georgia authority on outside access to DFCS records and the agency's status as an instrumentality of DHS. Cited in Spruill. It is the closest real Georgia authority for the oversight and records-access nodes (INP-09, FAIL-06, PMC-05), which currently rest on two mental-health and hospital-licensing cases with no child-welfare content.

GAP-CLOSING PASS, 2026-09-20: all eight authorities named as missing were located on CourtListener, retrieved, and read in this session; all eight are real, published, and on point, and all eight have been added below. No named authority failed verification. Two of the eight were mischaracterized in the gap list and are entered here on their actual holdings - see the State v. Jackson and M. D. H. notes.

Added Clark v. Wade, 273 Ga. 587 (2001), for ACT-04, OUT-03 and INP-05: it is the Supreme Court of Georgia's controlling narrowing construction of OCGA 19-7-1(b.1), requiring a third party to prove harm to the child by clear and convincing evidence before parental custody may be displaced, and it is the source of the rule that K. M. and Boddie apply.

Added Boddie v. Daniels, 288 Ga. 143 (2010), for INP-05 and OUT-01: it extends Clark's harm standard to OCGA 29-2-8(b) temporary guardianships, so a parent petitioning to end a guardianship need not prove anything and the guardian must prove clear and convincing harm from termination. It is equally on point for OUT-03 and ACT-04, which are at the six-case node_map cap; its relevance there is carried by Clark and K. M.

Added State v. Jackson, 269 Ga. 308 (1998), for DEC-03, FAIL-06, PMC-05 and INP-10: it is the Supreme Court of Georgia's first child abuse registry decision. CORRECTION to the gap list: Jackson did NOT hold that reputational stigma alone defeats a liberty interest. That sentence is the court's recitation of Paul v. Davis, which the court then distinguished; Jackson found a protected liberty interest, held the registry hearing procedure facially unconstitutional for barring compelled testimony of children under 14, and struck down the entire Act, OCGA 49-5-180 et seq. Steiner, 303 Ga. 890 (2018), reached the opposite result on a rebuilt statute and a different record, and the two must be read together.

Added Nix v. Department of Human Resources, 236 Ga. 794 (1976), for DEC-05: answering a certified question, it holds that an indigent parent appealing a termination order is entitled to a transcript at public expense because the Juvenile Code intends effective representation at all stages. It is equally on point for FAIL-01, which is at the six-case node_map cap alongside M. L. B., its federal analogue.

Added In the Interest of M. D. H., 300 Ga. 46 (2016), for DEC-05, INP-12 and OUT-05: it is the Supreme Court of Georgia's rule that a missed Juvenile Code filing deadline produces dismissal without prejudice absent an express legislative direction otherwise. CORRECTION to the gap list: M. D. H. is a DELINQUENCY case construing the 30-day petition deadline of OCGA 15-11-521(b), not a dependency case, and it does not construe OCGA 15-11-181(a). Its reasoning is expressly generalized to Juvenile Code deadlines and it collects the dependency-side authorities (Sanchez; In the Interest of E. C.), which is why it is mapped here; do not cite it as a dependency-timing holding.

Added Bendiburg v. Dempsey, 909 F.2d 463 (11th Cir. 1990), for ACT-06, DEC-04, INP-07, FAIL-02 and INP-12: a Georgia case holding that an ex parte custody transfer permitting a non-consented medical procedure is constitutional only in extraordinary circumstances with an adequate post-deprivation remedy, and that private clinicians who reach an understanding with DFACS caseworkers to obtain such an order are liable as joint actors under section 1983. This was the single largest gap in the brief and it brings ACT-06 to three cases.

Added Floyd County Grand Jury v. Department of Family & Children Services, 218 Ga. App. 832 (1995), for INP-09, FAIL-06, PMC-05, PMC-02 and INP-04: it holds county DFACS offices to be instrumentalities of the state DHR, not county offices, so a grand jury cannot civilly investigate or subpoena them. It replaces the mental-health and hospital cases as the closest real Georgia child-welfare authority on outside oversight and records access.

Added Perdue v. Kenny A. ex rel. Winn, 559 U.S. 542 (2010), for PMC-01 and PMC-02: it is the United States Supreme Court decision in the Georgia foster-care class action, holding that a section 1988 lodestar may be enhanced for superior performance only in rare and exceptional circumstances on specific evidence. NOTE on the gap list's citator concern: the reconciled brief contains no Kenny A. case entry (the Eleventh Circuit decision is referenced only in a note), so no citator failure is being propagated; Perdue is added on its own terms and as the mandatory subsequent history for any future Kenny A. entry.

Added Mandt v. Lovell, 293 Ga. 807 (2013), for ACT-05: this closes the gap the prior pass recorded as having no Georgia authority. It is the Supreme Court of Georgia's decision on the family violence protective order under OCGA 19-13-4 - the principal Georgia device for removing an abuser rather than the child - holding such an order a continuing judgment modifiable only on proof by a preponderance of a material change making renewed violence unlikely.

Added In the Interest of J. C. W., 318 Ga. App. 772 (2012), for OUT-04, ACT-04 and OUT-03: it is the closest published Georgia authority located on the age-18 terminus of a child-welfare custody disposition, holding that a long-term custody order runs to the eighteenth birthday, that the children are real parties in interest who may appeal it, and that the former Juvenile Code created no relative-placement preference. It applies the pre-2014 Code (OCGA 15-11-58(i)(1)); the node_map placement for OUT-04 is at ACT-04 and OUT-03's six-case cap, so those two nodes carry Clark and the existing kinship line.

Clark v. Wade was decided without a majority opinion. The quote is from the lead (plurality) opinion of Fletcher, P.J. The Supreme Court of Georgia itself, in Boddie v. Daniels, 288 Ga. at 145, states that 'the plurality opinion clearly represented the views of a majority of Justices on several points' and treats the narrowing construction quoted here as controlling; Boddie, a unanimous decision, is the safer citation for the same rule.

Convention note for readers: node_map is a curated list of at most six cases per node, as in the source brief. Several case entries carry relevance sentences for additional nodes where that node's node_map slot is already full (OUT-02, FAIL-01, ACT-04 and OUT-03 are at the six-case cap). Those relevance sentences are accurate and usable; the node_map simply records the six strongest authorities per decision point.

Every one of the 42 nodes now carries between two and six cases. The four nodes recorded as empty in the prior node_map (INP-04, INP-05, ACT-05, OUT-04) were a bookkeeping omission, not a research gap: the relevance objects of the existing case entries already covered them, and those entries have now been written into node_map along with the new authorities.

No named authority could not be verified. Two searches in this pass returned no usable Georgia authority and no case was added on them: Georgia appellate case law on CAPTA Citizen Review Panels (PMC-03), which remains mapped to Suter v. Artist M. and Steiner, and Georgia case law on children missing from foster care. Both remain genuine gaps in on-point state authority.

Missing (for a later pass): Maddox v. Stephens, 727 F.3d 1109 (11th Cir. 2013) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 1038256, decided 2013-08-21). A GEORGIA case (Wilkinson County DFCS) on a caseworker's removal of a child and the qualified-immunity analysis surrounding an ex parte custody order, and the single most glaring absence in the brief. The brief's own Bendiburg gap note asserts that Bendiburg 'is cited in Maddox, which the brief already uses' — but there is NO Maddox case entry anywhere in the brief. That is an internal inconsistency in the research record, and it leaves DEC-04, FAIL-02 and INP-12 without the most recent Eleventh Circuit application of the removal standard to Georgia facts.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the United States Supreme Court's controlling statement of the fundamental liberty interest of fit parents in the care, custody and control of their children, and the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interests. It is the constitutional premise on which Clark v. Wade's narrowing construction of OCGA 19-7-1(b.1) rests and which Boddie and K. M. carry forward. Its absence leaves ACT-04, OUT-03 and INP-05 resting on state-law constructions without the federal rule that compelled them.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — the foundational federal holding that an unwed father is entitled to a hearing on fitness before his children may be taken from him, and that a presumption of unfitness based on marital status violates due process and equal protection. It is the direct constitutional ancestor of In re Baby Girl Eason, which the brief cites for OUT-02 and INP-05 without its federal source, and it is the general authority that removal of a child from any parent requires an individualized unfitness determination.

Missing (for a later pass): Authority on OCGA 19-7-5(f)-(g) reporter immunity — the brief expressly concedes (Cechman note) that no Supreme Court of Georgia decision on the good-faith immunity provision was located. That concession is honest, but INP-01, INP-02, INP-06, INP-07 and INP-08 all turn on reporter liability and immunity, and the brief currently answers every one of them with Cechman's 1991 construction of a statute amended at least as recently as Ga. L. 2012, p. 239. Before this brief is relied on, the current text of OCGA 19-7-5 (reporter list, 24-hour deadline, immunity) must be checked directly and any post-2012 appellate construction run down.
